description: Common digraphs include ch, th, wh, and sh.
applies_when: word contains a common digraph such as ch th wh sh or a similar two-letter sound spelling

description: Common blends include bl, br, sc, sp, cl, cr, scr, squ, fl, dr, sm, st, gl, fr, sn, sw, pl, gr, sl, pr, tr.
applies_when: word begins or ends with a consonant blend and the child may drop or swap one sound

description: Some common silent-letter patterns are kn, wr, mb, and silent t in words like fasten.
applies_when: word contains a known silent-letter pattern such as kn wr mb or silent t

description: Schwa is an unstressed vowel sound, often heard in the first or last vowel of a word.
applies_when: unstressed syllable vowel

description: c sounds like /s/ before e, i, or y; otherwise c usually sounds like /k/.
applies_when: contains "c" followed by e, i, or y

description: g sounds like /j/ before e, i, or y; otherwise g usually keeps its hard sound.
applies_when: contains "g" followed by e, i, or y

description: When two vowels go walking, the first one often does the talking.
applies_when: word contains a common two-vowel team where the first vowel may carry the main sound

description: ea sometimes uses the short e sound.
applies_when: word contains ea and it says short e instead of the more expected long e sound

description: W can control nearby vowels a, o, and e and change their sound.
examples: crawl; straw; allow; brow; drew; blew
applies_when: word has w next to a o or e and the vowel sound changes because of w

description: Q is always followed by u; in this case u is not counted as a vowel.
applies_when: word contains q and the spelling choice after q is being considered

description: No native English words end with i, u, v, or j.
applies_when: word-final spelling choice would otherwise leave the word ending in i u v or j

description: When a word ends with a short vowel followed by one consonant, double the consonant before adding ed.
applies_when: adding the past-tense suffix -ed to a one-syllable base word with short vowel + single final consonant

pattern: base word ending in two consonants
description: When a word ends with two consonants, just add ed.
applies_when: adding the past-tense suffix -ed to a base word ending in two consonants

pattern: base word ending in letter e
description: When a word ends with e, just add d.
applies_when: adding the past-tense suffix -ed to a base word that already ends in silent e

description: When a word ends with a short vowel followed by one consonant, double the consonant before adding ing.
applies_when: adding the suffix -ing to a one-syllable base word with short vowel + single final consonant

pattern: base word ending in two consonants
description: When a word ends with two consonants, just add ing.
applies_when: adding the suffix -ing to a base word ending in two consonants

pattern: base word ending in letter e
description: Drop final e before adding ing.
applies_when: adding the suffix -ing to a base word ending in silent e

description: C is typically followed by a, o, u, l, or r in these patterns where it makes the /k/ sound.
applies_when: spelling choice is between c and k before a o u l or r

description: K is followed by i and e in these patterns.
applies_when: spelling choice is between c and k before i or e

description: When a one-syllable word ends in y, it usually says /ī/.
applies_when: one-syllable base word ends in y and the final sound is long i

description: Y says /ē/ at the end of a multi-syllable base word.
applies_when: multisyllable base word ends in y and the final sound is long e

description: AY usually spells /ā/ at the end of a base word.
applies_when: word ends with the long a sound and the spelling choice is between ai and ay

description: A final silent e can make the vowel say its name, even when one consonant stands in the way.
applies_when: word ends in a vowel-consonant-silent e pattern where the vowel is long

description: A final silent e usually cannot make the vowel long when two consonants stand between the vowel and the e.
applies_when: word has two consonants between the vowel and final e so the silent e does not make the vowel long

description: Final e can also make c say /s/ and g say /j/.
examples: cent; face; dance; wage; orange; gentle
applies_when: word uses final e to soften c to /s/ or g to /j/

description: If the final /ch/ sound comes after a consonant, the ending is usually -ch.
applies_when: word ends with the /ch/ sound after a consonant

description: When final /ch/ follows a one-letter vowel, it is usually written -tch.
exceptions: attach; much; sandwich; which; detach; ostrich; spinach; enrich; rich; such
applies_when: word ends with the /ch/ sound after a single short vowel

description: Some words do not use -tch even after a one-letter vowel.
examples: attach; much; sandwich; which; detach; ostrich; spinach; enrich; rich; such
applies_when: word ends with the /ch/ sound after a single vowel but belongs to a known -ch exception family

description: tch is used only after a single vowel that does not say its name.
exceptions: attach; much; sandwich; which; detach; ostrich; spinach; enrich; rich; such
applies_when: word ends with the /ch/ sound after a single short vowel

description: If the final /ch/ sound comes after a two-letter vowel, the ending is usually -ch.
applies_when: word ends with the /ch/ sound after a two-letter vowel team

description: Add e to keep singular words that end in one s from looking plural.
applies_when: base word ends in a single final s and needs an e to avoid looking plural

description: Double the last consonant when adding a vowel suffix to words ending in one vowel followed by one consonant.
applies_when: adding a vowel-initial suffix to a base word with short vowel + single final consonant

description: dge is used only after a single vowel that says its short sound.
applies_when: word ends with the /j/ sound after a single short vowel

description: Change y to i when adding an ending, unless the ending begins with i.
applies_when: adding a suffix to a base word ending in consonant + y unless the suffix begins with i

description: Do not change y to i when the ending begins with i; skiing is listed as an exception example.
applies_when: adding a suffix that begins with i to a word where changing y or adjacent vowels would create an incorrect form

description: To make a noun plural, add -s unless the word hisses or changes, then add -es.
applies_when: forming a plural noun from a singular base word

description: To make a verb third person singular, add -s unless the word hisses, then add -es.
applies_when: forming the third-person singular present-tense verb

description: The prefix all is written with one l (al) before another syllable.
applies_when: word begins with the prefix al meaning all

description: CK is used only after a single vowel that says its short sound.
applies_when: ends with "ck" after short vowel

description: F, L, and S are often doubled after a single vowel at the end of a base word.
examples: class; fall; gruff; hiss; doll; stuff
applies_when: base word ends with f l or s after a single vowel

description: full is written with one l (ful) when added as a suffix.
applies_when: word uses the suffix -ful

description: O may say /ŭ/ in a stressed syllable next to th, m, n, or v.
applies_when: word has o next to th m n or v and the vowel says schwa or short u

description: The /sh/ sound can be spelled sh, ci, ti, si, ch, or ssi, often in certain endings.
examples: tion; tious; tial; cian; cial; cious; sion; ssion
applies_when: word contains the /sh/ sound and the spelling choice involves sh ci ti si ch or ssi

description: In long words, especially Greek-origin words, the /f/ sound may be spelled ph.
applies_when: word contains the /f/ sound in a Greek-origin or Greek-pattern word and the spelling may be ph

description: Use oi at the beginning or in the middle of a word for the /oi/ sound; use oy at the end.
applies_when: word contains the /oi/ sound; if the /oi/ sound is at the beginning or in the middle of the word choose oi; if the /oi/ sound is at the end of the word choose oy

description: Use ou at the beginning or in the middle of a word for the /ou/ sound; use ow at the end.
applies_when: word contains the /ou/ sound; if the /ou/ sound is at the beginning or in the middle of the word choose ou; if the /ou/ sound is at the end of the word choose ow

description: A, E, O, and U usually say their long sounds at the end of an open syllable.
applies_when: word has an open syllable ending in a vowel and the vowel says its long sound

description: I and Y may say either short /i/ or long /i/ at the end of a syllable, depending on the word.
applies_when: word ends a syllable with i or y and the vowel sound must be judged from the word family or pronunciation

description: I may say /e/ with a silent final e, at the end of a syllable, or at the end of some foreign words.
applies_when: word has i in an open syllable or final i in a known pattern where it says long e

description: I and O may sometimes say their long sounds before two consonants like -nd or -ld or -st or -lt.
applies_when: word contains i or o before two consonants and the vowel is one of the known long-vowel family patterns such as mind most old or find

description: A may say /ah/ at the end of a word, after w, or before l.
applies_when: word has a at the end of a word after w or before l and the vowel says /ah/

description: A final e can keep a singular word ending in s from looking plural.
applies_when: word ends in a singular final s pattern where silent e prevents the word from looking plural

description: A final e can be kept or added to make a word clearer in meaning or easier to distinguish.
applies_when: final e helps distinguish the word from another form or keeps the spelling visually clear

description: A final e can help signal the voiced /th/ sound in some words.
applies_when: word ends with the voiced /th/ sound and final e helps signal that pronunciation

description: Two i letters normally do not stand next to each other in English words.
applies_when: spelling choice would otherwise place two i letters next to each other in an English word

description: TI, CI, and SI are typically used at the beginning of a syllable after the first one.
applies_when: word has the /sh/ or /zh/ sound at the start of a later syllable and the spelling choice is ti ci or si

description: SH usually spells /sh/ at the beginning of a base word or the end of a syllable, but not at the start of later syllables except in -ship.
applies_when: word has the /sh/ sound at the beginning of a base word or the end of a syllable

description: The past-tense ending -ed forms a new syllable after /d/ or /t/; otherwise it is pronounced /d/ or /t/.
applies_when: explaining how the past-tense suffix -ed is pronounced after a base word

description: Phonograms ending in gh are usually found at the end of a base word or before t; gh may be silent or say /f/.
applies_when: word contains gh at the end of a base word or before t

description: At the beginning of a base word, /z/ is typically spelled with z rather than s.
applies_when: word begins with the /z/ sound and the spelling choice is between z and s

description: Any vowel may say a schwa sound in an unstressed syllable or unstressed word.
applies_when: word has an unstressed syllable where the vowel reduces to schwa

description: O may say schwa /uh/ in a stressed syllable when next to w, th, m, n, or v.
applies_when: word has o next to w th m n or v and the vowel reduces toward schwa or short u

description: AR and OR may reduce to a schwa-like /er/ sound in an unstressed syllable.
applies_when: word has ar or or in an unstressed syllable and the sound reduces toward /er/
